pages.title: Getting Started
pages.content:
We are getting started with C++! Let’s begin by greeting the world and learning how to write a simple program in C++. This will be our first program, and through it, we'll explore the basics of C++ syntax.

Once we see our message printed, we will break it down step by step, understanding each part of the program and how C++ processes it. This will set the foundation for everything we’ll learn in C++!

---

**Example:**
```cpp
cout<<"Hello World"; // cout is the print statement in c++
```
**Output:**
```default
Hello World
```

pages.title: Understanding Your First C++ Program
pages.content:
Let’s explore the structure of your very first C++ program — the classic **"Hello, World!"**. It’s simple, but it gives us a peek into how C++ works behind the scenes.
```cpp
#include 

using namespace std;

int main() {
    cout `
This line tells the compiler to include the input-output stream library. It's what allows us to use `cout` to display messages on the screen. Think of it as plugging in a speaker before you can talk.

- `using namespace std;`
This line helps avoid writing `std::cout` every time. You're telling C++ to use the **standard namespace** for all built-in features, like `cout` and `endl`. It’s like saying “Just call me by my nickname.”

- `int main() { ... }`
This is the **starting point** of your program. Every C++ program begins here. You can think of `main()` as the entrance to a house—without it, your program has nowhere to begin.

- `cout << "Hello, World!" << endl;`
This prints text to the console. It’s your way of telling the computer: “Hey, show this message!” The `<<` operator passes the message into the output stream, and `endl` moves to the next line.

- `return 0;`
This line tells the operating system, “Everything ran fine.” It signals that the program ended successfully.

Don’t worry if this feels like a lot! As we move forward, we’ll explore each part in more detail. For now, just get comfortable with how things are structured. You’ve just written your first C++ program!

pages.title: Comments in C++
pages.content:
In C++, comments are non-executable text added to improve code readability. They help explain what the code does, why it was written in a certain way, or provide notes for future reference. The compiler ignores comments, so they don’t affect how the program runs.

Remember, good comments explain the intent behind the code, not just what the code is doing. Use them to clarify complex logic, describe important decisions, or offer helpful context for other developers.

---

**C++ supports two types of comments**
1. **Single-line Comments** These start with // and are used for short, inline explanations.
```cpp
// This is a single-line comment
std::cout << "Hello, World!" << std::endl;
```

2. **Multi-line Comments** These start with /* and end with */, and are ideal for longer explanations that span several lines.
```cpp
/* This is a multi-line comment
   It can span across multiple lines
   and explain code in more detail */
std::cout << "Hello, World!" << std::endl;
```

pages.title: Identifiers in C++
pages.content:
* Identifiers are **names given by the programmer** to elements like:
  * Variables
  * Functions
  * Classes
* They are used to **uniquely identify** parts of the program.
* For example, `main` is an identifier that names the function where execution starts.
* We will learn more about functions and variables later, where you'll see how identifiers are used in real programs.

---

**Rules for Creating Identifiers:**

* Must **start with a letter** (A–Z or a–z) or an **underscore** (`_`)
* Can contain **letters, digits (0–9)**, and **underscores**
* Cannot use **C++ keywords** like `int`, `return`, `if` as identifiers
* **Case-sensitive**: `score`, `Score`, and `SCORE` are treated as different identifiers

---

**Examples of Valid and Invalid Identifiers:**

```cpp
int age = 25;         // Valid (starts with a letter)
int _score = 90;      // Valid (starts with an underscore)
int number1 = 100;    // Valid (contains letters and digits)

// int int = 5;       // Invalid: 'int' is a keyword
// int 2value = 50;   // Invalid: Cannot start with a digit
// int return = 10;   // Invalid: 'return' is a keyword
```

**Don't worry if you don't understand variables yet — we'll cover variables and how to use them in upcoming lessons.**

pages.title: Escape Sequences in C++
pages.content:
In this lesson, you'll learn about escape characters in C++. In C++, when you want to include special characters inside a string, you can use **"escape sequences."**
An escape sequence starts with a backslash (`\`) followed by a character. This tells the C++ compiler to treat that combination as a special character, rather than normal text.

---

**Example:**
```cpp
#include  // Includes the Input/Output stream library

using namespace std; 

int main() {
    // Output the character 'A' followed by a newline
    cout << 'A' << '\n';    // '\n' represents a newline character
    // Output the character 'B', followed by a tab space, then the character 'C', and a newline
    cout << 'B' << '\t' << 'C' << '\n'; // '\t' represents a tab character

    // Indicates successful program termination
    return 0;
}
```
**Output:**
```default
A
B   C
```

---

**Common Escape Sequences in C++**
1. `\n` - Moves the cursor to the beginning of the next line.
2. `\t` - Inserts a horizontal tab.
3. `\\` - Inserts a backslash character.
4. `\"` - Inserts a double quote character within a string.
5. `\'` - Inserts a single quote character.

pages.title: Getting started with programming problems
pages.content:
If you are here - then you should already know the basic syntax of C++.

If not, then head to the [Learn C++ course](https://www.codechef.com/learn/course/cpp) and finish it once.

Let's now take it up a notch and train you to solve programming problems. Before that, let us do a quick recap of what we had learned about C++ in [Learn C++ Path](https://www.codechef.com/learn/course/cpp).

On CodeChef and other platforms, you will come across programming problems.
- Each programming problem has a **problem statement**
- You write a **solution code** which will solve the problem
- Your code is run, does some computation and generates **your output**
- **Your output** is compared with the **Expected output**. 
  - If they match - then your code is correct!
  - If they don't match - then there is some error in your code.

Click on **Next** to proceed!

practiceProblems.title: Data Types
practiceProblems.description:
Lets look at some common data types found in programming problems for beginners

- Integers
  - Integers are whole numbers that can be negative, zero or positive. Examples - **15**, **0**, **-5**

- Float
  - A float will have a decimal place. Examples - **4.5**, **-2.778**
  - Note that **4.0**, **-2.0** are also floats

- Strings
  - Strings are a group of characters. Examples - **abcde**, **SEED-IT**, **START69**
  - Note that strings can also contain numerical characters. Examples **a1b2c3d4**, **532**

- Arrays 
  - Arrays are used to store multiple variables of the same data type. Examples of arrays
     - Array containing 6 integers - **[1 , 5, 7, 10, 15, 2]**

practiceProblems.title: How to accept multiple inputs in a line
practiceProblems.description:
Sometimes - we have to accept multiple inputs in a single line.\
We can use the same syntax to accept multiple inputs in a single line, however the different inputs will be separated by a **'>>'** operator.

The syntax for the same is as follows -

     cin >> a >> b >> c;   # assigns input values to variables a, b and c

Now lets try and solve the following
- Accept 3 space separated integers given in a line into 3 variables - $A$, $B$ and $C$
- Print them out to a single line on the console

You can play around with the exact syntax in the IDE -> refer to the solution in case you are unable to get this correct. \
Code the solution in the IDE and then click **Submit** to continue.

practiceProblems.title: Difference between Run and Submit
practiceProblems.description:
What is the difference between the  **`Run`**  and  **`Submit`**  buttons?
- **`Run`**  allows you to locally test your code on  **`sample inputs`**  and  **`custom inputs`**
   - `Custom inputs`  are small inputs - mainly for you to test your code
- **`Submit`**  sends your code to the online judge to compare your  **`Actual output`**  and the  **`Expected output`**
   - On submission - your code is checked against thousands of  `test cases`  which are included in the 
**hidden** or **private** test files
   - Your code / solution is complete only when you click  **`Submit`**  and get an  **`AC`**  (accepted) verdict
   - **Note:** Your code can run as expected for your  `custom inputs`  - however, it can fail on the **private** 
 `test files`. \
This means your code is **NOT** solving the problem correctly and needs to be fixed.
### Task
You are given a program which does the following
- Accepts the count of  `test cases`  -  ***`t`***  - in the 1st line. \
First line of each  `test case`  consists of an integer  ***`N`***
- Outputs the integer which is greater than  ***`N`***  by  ***`1`***
- Click on  **`Run`**  to check the result on  `custom inputs`
- Click on  **`Submit`**  to check the final verdict
